extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in politics, media, technology, and disinformation
extracted.subtask_description: An opinion/news article analyzing a specific social-media propaganda campaign (Bell Pottinger/Guptas) and comparing it to Cambridge Analytica-style data-driven influence operations. Discusses tactics, effects, and remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of mixed actors (real people, bots, websites)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Their campaign entailed using real people, Twitter bots and websites in an effort to portray the family as victims...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Campaigns that combine organic accounts and automated/synthetic actors amplify messaging and manufacture apparent grassroots support; identify whether messaging networks include both real accounts and bots to assess orchestration and reach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Targeting individual journalists
rubrics_metrics.description: “Individual journalists who were reporting on their corrupt deals were also targeted directly with the messaging.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Directly targeting reporters is a tactic aimed at intimidation, distraction, or reputational manipulation; evaluate whether actors singled out media figures and how that affected reporting and press freedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixing in elements of truth to increase susceptibility
rubrics_metrics.description: “Despite the crude tactics deployed by Bell Pottinger, their campaign clearly contained elements of truth, which made some people much more susceptible to their messages.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether falsehoods are blended with truthful claims — the presence of verifiable facts increases credibility and persuasiveness of disinformation; measure susceptibility when truth is mixed with distortion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploiting existing racial tensions and structural injustices
rubrics_metrics.description: “What Bell Pottinger’s campaign did was simply exploit already existing racial tensions based on legitimate concerns about racial injustice.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate campaigns for whether they leverage real social grievances (economic inequality, racial injustice) to amplify division; campaigns exploiting existing injustices are more effective and signal need for structural remedies, not only counter-messaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry/regulatory accountability (sanctions as indicator)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Bell Pottinger went on to receive the harshest sanction from the UK’s Public Relations and Communications Association (PRCA), a national industry association from which it was expelled.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use regulatory or industry actions (expulsion, sanctions) as evidence of wrongdoing and as part of assessing remedies; note that industry sanctions are one measure of accountability but may not address root harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data harvesting and profiling enable tailored influence
rubrics_metrics.description: “Recent revelations ... prompted concerns about privacy and data. It is certainly true that the harvesting of data has been used to develop profiling tools, which enable seemingly innocuous algorithms to inform people’s worldviews, as the information consumed is linked to personality traits.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether campaigns used data-driven profiling to segment audiences and deliver bespoke messages; the presence of targeted profiling indicates higher sophistication and privacy harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Less-sophisticated methods can still be effective
rubrics_metrics.description: “Using less sophisticated methods, Bell Pottinger ... was hired in 2016 ... to pave the way ... Their campaign entailed using real people, Twitter bots and websites ...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not equate sophistication with impact — simpler mixes of actors and tactics can still sway opinion when aligned with social conditions; evaluate impact, not just technical sophistication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Addressing root causes beyond removing bad actors
rubrics_metrics.description: “Eliminating groups like Cambridge Analytica or preventing the manipulation of data or use of bots to spread disinformation won’t end racism, misogyny and inequality; our societies must work together to target the root causes and end it ourselves.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing remedies, distinguish between removing malicious operators and addressing underlying social inequalities that make populations vulnerable to manipulation; prioritize policies that both limit manipulation and reduce structural vulnerabilities.
